Year 8 Enquiry • 1517–1689

Crown, Church, or Parliament?

The Struggle for Authority, Religion, and the English State (1517–1689)
Primary Visual Evidence • Tudor Royal Propaganda Hans Holbein the Younger (c. 1537)

Following the 1534 Act of Supremacy, Henry VIII commissioned Hans Holbein to project an overwhelming image of absolute monarchical sovereignty. Every visual element was calculated statecraft:

1. Stance of Absolute Dominance:
Facing the viewer squarely with feet planted wide, elbows flared, and hands gripping dagger and gloves, Henry occupies maximum physical space to intimidate foreign ambassadors and subjects.
2. Imperial Splendour & Monastic Wealth:
Exaggerated square shoulders padded in ermine fur, gold-embroidered silver doublet, and heavy ruby collars—lavishly financed by Thomas Cromwell’s Dissolution of the Monasteries (1536–40).
3. Dynastic Virility & Tudor Succession:
The prominent codpiece and muscular posture were deliberate visual propaganda, asserting vitality and the promise of a legitimate male Tudor heir following the break with Rome.
4. The Absent Pope (Sovereignty Unchallenged):
Depicted with zero papal, cross, or Roman Catholic emblems. The King stands solitary on English ground—the undisputed Supreme Head on Earth of the Church of England.
The Dagger
Immediate physical violence against papal traitors.
Ermine & Gold
Imperial status equal to Holy Roman Emperor.
Turkish Carpet
Global trade connections & Renaissance wealth.
Disciplinary Significance: In 16th-century England, lacking a standing army or police force, visual portraiture was essential constitutional statecraft to enforce Royal Supremacy.
Disciplinary Hinge Question: Historical Evaluation
Does this portrait show a monarch completely confident in his sovereign power, or a ruler using theatrical spectacle to mask profound dynastic and religious vulnerability?
Primary Visual Evidence: Full-Length Portrait of King Henry VIII • Workshop of Hans Holbein the Younger (c. 1537–1540) ROYAL COLLECTION ARCHIVE • WALKER ART GALLERY
1. Explaining Why Events Happened [12 Marks]

2. Core Skills & Source Workshops [4m & 8m]
Four dedicated source investigations: test written statutes and visual propaganda for utility; practise features and differences (5–12 mins).
3. Big Enquiry Essay: Reaching a Verdict [16+4m]
Enquiry 5: ‘How far do you agree?’ Reach a reasoned historical verdict weighing the power of Crown, Church, and Parliament across 172 years (25 mins).

ENQUIRY 1 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • CROWN, CHURCH, OR PARLIAMENT? (1517–1689)

Why did Henry VIII break with Rome, and how was Royal Supremacy established?

Core Specification Focus: Break with Rome; Royal Supremacy; Act of Supremacy (1534); Dynastic and financial causes.
Chronological Inquiry Spine • Core Causal Narrative Take structured notes alongside each stage as your teacher narrates the history
1 1517–1527 • Why did the royal marriage become an urgent dynastic crisis?
• Catherine of Aragon had no surviving male heir to secure the Tudor succession
• Henry VIII feared a divine curse from God, citing Leviticus 20:21
• Anne Boleyn refused to be a royal mistress, demanding legitimate marriage
2 1527–1529 • Why did Pope Clement VII refuse Henry’s annulment request?
• Cardinal Wolsey failed to secure a papal annulment from Rome
• In 1527, Charles V sacked Rome and held Pope Clement captive
• Charles V was Catherine’s nephew, blocking any divorce from Henry
3 1529–1532 • How did Thomas Cromwell use Parliament to pressure the Church?
• Thomas Cromwell advised Henry to break England from the legal power of Rome
• Reformation Parliament passed laws attacking church abuses and clergy privileges
• In 1532, English bishops surrendered their independence to the King
4 1533 • How did the Act in Restraint of Appeals make England an ‘Empire’?
• 1533 statute declared: ‘This realm of England is an Empire’ under the King alone
• Banned all English legal and religious appeals to the Pope in Rome
• Archbishop Cranmer annulled Henry’s marriage; Anne Boleyn crowned Queen
5 1534 • How did the Act of Supremacy legally consolidate royal sovereignty?
• 1534 Act of Supremacy declared Henry the ‘Supreme Head’ of the Church of England
• Treason Act made denying the King’s supremacy punishable by public execution
• Sir Thomas More and Bishop Fisher were beheaded for refusing the oath
2/24 In 1534, questioning Henry VIII’s marriage was high treason punishable by death at Tower Hill.

ENQUIRY 2 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • CROWN, CHURCH, OR PARLIAMENT? (1517–1689)

How did Elizabeth I navigate religious divisions through the 1559 Via Media?

Core Specification Focus: Elizabethan Religious Settlement (1559); Act of Supremacy; Act of Uniformity; Via Media compromise.
Chronological Inquiry Spine • Core Causal Narrative Take structured notes alongside each stage as your teacher narrates the history
1 1558–1559 • Why was England religiously fractured when Elizabeth became Queen?
• Violent religious swings under Edward VI (Protestant) and Mary I (Catholic)
• Over 280 Protestants burned at the stake under Mary I, sparking deep anti-Catholic fear
• Returning Protestant exiles demanded radical reform, while Catholics held the north
2 1559 • How did the Act of Supremacy restore royal control through compromise?
• Elizabeth dropped Henry VIII’s title of ‘Supreme Head’ to avoid offending Catholics
• Adopted the compromise title of ‘Supreme Governor’ of the Church of England
• All clergy took an Oath of Supremacy; all but one Catholic bishop refused and were dismissed
3 1559 • How did the Act of Uniformity establish the ‘Middle Way’ (Via Media)?
• Set up a single national church using the 1559 English Book of Common Prayer
• Communion wording was kept ambiguous so Protestants and Catholics could accept it
• Compulsory church attendance; recusants who stayed away paid a 12d shilling fine
4 1568–1570 • How did Mary Queen of Scots and the Papal Bull spark Catholic plots?
• In 1568, Catholic cousin Mary Queen of Scots fled to England and became a rival figurehead
• Northern Catholic Earls rebelled in 1569, attempting to overthrow Elizabeth and free Mary
• In 1570, Pope Pius V excommunicated Elizabeth, ordering Catholics to depose her
5 1571–1588 • How did Walsingham’s spy network lead to Mary’s execution?
• Sir Francis Walsingham built a network of spies and codebreakers to uncover Catholic plots
• Babington Plot (1586) intercepted letter proving Mary agreed to assassinate Elizabeth
• Elizabeth reluctantly signed the death warrant; Mary was beheaded in February 1587
4/24 Elizabeth I had ‘no desire to make windows into men’s souls’—pay your Sunday fines and keep private doubts to yourself.

Tudor Source Workshop 1: Henry VIII & Royal Supremacy (1534)

Question 3(a): How Useful [8 marks • 10–12 mins]
How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into how King Henry VIII established Royal Supremacy over the Church of England?
SOURCE A: Official Statute • The Act of Supremacy (November 1534) Contemporary Written Evidence
“Albeit the King’s Majesty justly and rightfully is and ought to be the supreme head of the Church of England... be it enacted by authority of this present Parliament that the King our sovereign lord, his heirs and successors kings of this realm, shall be taken, accepted, and reputed the only supreme head in earth of the Church of England... and shall have full power to correct and reform all manner of errors, heresies, and abuses within the same.”
Provenance Analysis:
• Nature: Official Act of Parliament with full force of English statutory law.
• Origin: Drafted by Thomas Cromwell and passed by the Reformation Parliament.
• Purpose: Legally assert supreme royal authority and deter papal resistance under threat of high treason.
1. Source A Evaluation • Content & Provenance: (What does Source A prove about how Henry VIII made his religious supremacy legally binding upon all subjects?)
SOURCE B: Contemporary Woodcut • Title Page of the Great Bible (1539) Contemporary Visual Evidence
Iconography & Visual Evidence:
• 1. Divine Authority: God in heaven blesses King Henry, who sits crowned on his throne.
• 2. Royal Supremacy: Henry hands the Bible directly to Cranmer (Church) and Cromwell (Nobility).
• 3. Eradication of the Pope: The Pope is completely absent from the national religious hierarchy.
• 4. Popular Obedience: Subjects at the base shout ‘Vivat Rex’ and ‘God Save the King’.
Title page of the Great Bible (1539), commissioned by Thomas Cromwell and authorized by King Henry VIII for every parish church in England.
2. Source B Evaluation • Visual Evidence & Purpose: (What visual message does Source B communicate about the King’s new position as head of both Church and State?)
3. Comparative Utility Verdict • Final Synthesis: (Compare both sources • Which provides greater historical insight into this enquiry, and why?)
Structure Strip: Para 1: Source A (Content + Provenance: statutory parliamentary authority) • Para 2: Source B (Visual Evidence + Purpose: royal propaganda of divine kingship) • Verdict: Explain how combining legal statute with visual propaganda secured total Crown control.
6/24 Henry VIII placed his face on every English Bible so no subject could ever forget who ran the Church.

Tudor Source Workshop 2: Elizabeth I & Royal Authority (1559–1588)

Question 3(a): How Useful [8 marks • 10–12 mins]
How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into how Elizabeth I maintained authority and religious stability in England?
SOURCE A: Official Statute • The Act of Uniformity (April 1559) Contemporary Written Evidence
“Every person and persons inhabiting within this realm shall diligently and faithfully, having no lawful or reasonable excuse to be absent, endeavour themselves to resort to their parish church... upon every Sunday and other days ordained to be kept as holy days, upon pain that every person so offending shall forfeit for every such offence twelve pence, to be levied by the churchwardens to the use of the poor.”
Provenance Analysis:
• Nature: Parliamentary statute establishing compulsory national church attendance.
• Origin: Elizabethan government legislative compromise (The Via Media).
• Purpose: Enforce outward religious uniformity while avoiding Marian heresy burnings or open civil rebellion.
1. Source A Evaluation • Content & Provenance: (What does Source A reveal about Elizabeth’s strategy of demanding outward obedience through fines rather than religious persecution?)
SOURCE B: Royal Portraiture • The Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I (c. 1588) Contemporary Visual Evidence
Iconography & Visual Evidence:
• 1. Global Dominion: Elizabeth’s hand rests firmly on the globe, asserting English power over the Americas.
• 2. Imperial Crown: Sits prominently behind the Queen, symbolizing independent imperial majesty.
• 3. Providential Victory: Windows show the calm English fleet on the left, and Spanish galleons wrecked on the right.
• 4. Virgin Purity: Pearls and bows symbolize chastity, national security, and God’s sacred protection.
The Armada Portrait (c. 1588), commemorating the defeat of Philip II’s invasion fleet and celebrating Elizabeth’s providential rule.
2. Source B Evaluation • Visual Evidence & Purpose: (How does Source B use visual symbols to convince English subjects that Elizabeth was chosen and protected by God?)
3. Comparative Utility Verdict • Final Synthesis: (Compare both sources • Which provides greater historical insight into this enquiry, and why?)
Structure Strip: Para 1: Source A (Content + Provenance: pragmatic legal fines) • Para 2: Source B (Visual Evidence + Purpose: providential imperial propaganda) • Verdict: Weigh how statutory compromise and visual myth-making together secured national stability.
Elizabeth I demanded 12-pence Sunday fines for missed church—expensive enough to enforce conformity without provoking martyrs. 7/24
ENQUIRY 3 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • CROWN, CHURCH, OR PARLIAMENT? (1517–1689)

Why was Philip II’s Armada defeated, and how did naval strategy transform warfare?

Core Specification Focus: Anglo-Spanish rivalry; execution of Mary Queen of Scots (1587); Armada campaign; naval tactics and weather.
Chronological Inquiry Spine • Core Causal Narrative Take structured notes alongside each stage as your teacher narrates the history
1 1585–1587 • What imperial and religious rivalries provoked Philip II’s invasion?
• Philip II was determined to restore Catholicism and punish England for Mary’s execution
• Francis Drake and English privateers repeatedly plundered Spanish treasure ships
• Elizabeth sent English troops to help Protestant Dutch rebels fight against Spain
2 1587 • How did Drake’s raid on Cadiz delay the Spanish invasion?
• In April 1587, Drake sailed daringly into Cadiz harbor in southern Spain
• Burned over 30 Spanish warships and destroyed seasoned barrel wood supplies
• Drake boasted he had ‘singed the King of Spain’s beard’, delaying the Armada by a year
3 July 1588 • How did the English fleet harry the Armada up the English Channel?
• 130 Spanish ships sailed in an impenetrable crescent formation up the English Channel
• English race-built galleons were faster, lighter, and loaded long-range culverin cannon
• English gunners fired from safe distance, preventing Spanish soldiers from boarding
4 7–8 August 1588 • How did English fireships at Calais shatter the Spanish formation?
• Armada anchored off Calais waiting for the Duke of Parma’s army from Flanders
• At midnight on 7 August, the English launched eight blazing fireships into the fleet
• Spanish captains panicked, cut their heavy anchor cables, and scattered into the dark
5 Aug–Sept 1588 • How did the Battle of Gravelines and severe storms destroy the fleet?
• At Gravelines, English warships battered the scattered, anchorless Spanish galleons
• Ferocious Atlantic gales (‘The Protestant Wind’) drove the Armada around Scotland and Ireland
• Over 50 Spanish ships wrecked on rocky coasts; fewer than half limped home to Spain
8/24 The Armada carried 130 ships and 30,000 soldiers. Unfortunately for Philip II, none of it stopped English fireships.

ENQUIRY 4 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • CROWN, CHURCH, OR PARLIAMENT? (1517–1689)

Why did the collision over Divine Right lead to the trial and execution of Charles I?

Core Specification Focus: Causes of Civil War; Charles I Personal Rule (1629–40); New Model Army; Trial & Regicide (1649); Bill of Rights (1689).
Chronological Inquiry Spine • Core Causal Narrative Take structured notes alongside each stage as your teacher narrates the history
1 1629–1640 • Why did Charles I’s ‘Personal Rule’ without Parliament cause outrage?
• Charles I believed in Divine Right—that kings answer only to God, never to Parliament
• Ruled 11 years alone, raising archaic taxes like inland Ship Money without MPs’ consent
• Archbishop Laud forced English prayer books on Scotland, sparking an armed rebellion
2 1640–1642 • How did the breakdown of trust lead to armed civil conflict?
• Bankruptcy forced Charles to summon the Long Parliament; MPs arrested royal ministers
• In January 1642, Charles entered the Commons with 400 soldiers to arrest five MPs
• The MPs had fled; Charles raised the royal standard at Nottingham on 22 August 1642
3 1645–1648 • How did the New Model Army defeat the King at the Battle of Naseby?
• Parliament formed the New Model Army under Fairfax and Cromwell, promoted on merit
• Decisive victory at the Battle of Naseby (1645) destroyed Charles’s royalist army
• Defeated Charles secretly plotted with the Scots to invade England (Second Civil War, 1648)
4 1648–1649 • Why did Pride’s Purge and the High Court lead to regicide?
• In Dec 1648, Colonel Pride purged moderate MPs who wanted to negotiate with the King
• Remaining ‘Rump Parliament’ put Charles on trial for treason against his own people
• Charles refused to plead; publicly beheaded outside Whitehall on 30 January 1649
5 1660–1689 • How did the Glorious Revolution permanently limit royal power?
• Cromwell’s republic collapsed, restoring Charles II in 1660, but James II alienated MPs
• In 1688, Parliament invited Dutch Prince William of Orange to replace Catholic James II
• The 1689 Bill of Rights established that no monarch can tax or keep an army without Parliament
10/24 Charles I insisted no earthly court could try a king; three days later, Parliament had him beheaded outside Whitehall.

ENQUIRY 5 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • CROWN, CHURCH, OR PARLIAMENT? (1517–1689)

Which turning point decisively transformed the English state between 1517 and 1689?

Core Specification Focus: Synoptic evaluation of Royal Supremacy, Civil War, Regicide, and the 1689 Bill of Rights.
Chronological Inquiry Spine • Core Causal Narrative Take structured notes alongside each stage as your teacher narrates the history
1 1517–1534 • How did Henry VIII reshape sovereign authority in the Reformation?
• Henry broke with Rome to secure Tudor succession and Crown wealth
• 1534 Act of Supremacy used Parliament to give religious change legal authority
• Dissolution of monasteries created landed gentry invested in Protestant rule
2 1559–1588 • How did the Elizabethan settlement forge a Protestant national state?
• The 1559 Via Media compromise prevented the religious civil wars seen in Europe
• Queen governed as ‘Supreme Governor’ with broad popular acceptance and outward conformity
• Victory over the Spanish Armada in 1588 fused English patriotism with Protestantism
3 1603–1640 • Why did Stuart claims of Divine Right provoke constitutional crisis?
• James I and Charles I asserted absolute royal prerogative, claiming they answered only to God
• Charles I’s 11-Year Personal Rule raised illegal taxes and silenced critics without Parliament
• Attempt to impose religious uniformity sparked war with Scotland, bankrupting the King
4 1642–1649 • Why was the trial and execution of Charles I a radical turning point?
• Civil war proved a disciplined parliamentary citizen army could defeat the King’s forces
• Regicide in 1649 proved that an English monarch was accountable to the law of the people
• Abolishing the monarchy and House of Lords created England’s only republican Commonwealth
5 1660–1689 • How did the 1689 Bill of Rights finalize Parliamentary Supremacy?
• The 1660 Restoration failed to settle whether King or Parliament held supreme power
• Glorious Revolution (1688) expelled James II without major bloodshed
• 1689 Bill of Rights established parliamentary sovereignty: law and taxation require Parliament
14/24 In 1689, William III accepted the Bill of Rights to secure war taxes, legally subordinating the Crown to Parliament.

Stuart Source Workshop 3: Charles I & Divine Right on Trial (1649)

Question 3(a): How Useful [8 marks • 10–12 mins]
How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into why King Charles I was tried and executed in January 1649?
SOURCE A: Verbatim Court Transcript • Charles I at Westminster Hall (22 January 1649) Contemporary Written Evidence
“I would know by what power I am called hither... I would know by what authority, I mean lawful; for there are many unlawful authorities in the world, thieves and robbers by the highways... Remember I am your King, your lawful King! I have a trust committed unto me by God, by old and lawful descent; I will not betray it to answer to a new and unlawful authority. An earthly King cannot be tried by any court on earth!”
Provenance Analysis:
• Nature: Official trial courtroom speech spoken directly by the King.
• Origin: High Court of Justice proceedings, recorded by parliamentary court scribes.
• Purpose: Deny that any human court holds legal jurisdiction over an anointed monarch answering only to God.
1. Source A Evaluation • Content & Provenance: (What does Source A prove about Charles I’s unyielding refusal to compromise on the Divine Right of Kings?)
SOURCE B: Contemporary Broadside • Execution of Charles I at Whitehall (30 January 1649) Contemporary Visual Evidence
Iconography & Visual Evidence:
• 1. The Scaffold: Erected outside the royal Banqueting House at Whitehall.
• 2. The Severed Head: Executioner holds up the King’s head before a vast crowd.
• 3. Military Guard: New Model Army cavalry and pikemen surround the scaffold to prevent public rebellion.
• 4. Martyrdom Medallions: Top portraits frame Charles as a Christian martyr sacrifice.
Contemporary 1649 German broadside engraving depicting the public beheading of King Charles I outside the Banqueting House at Whitehall.
2. Source B Evaluation • Visual Evidence & Purpose: (What does Source B reveal about the public shock and military power required to carry out the King’s execution?)
3. Comparative Utility Verdict • Final Synthesis: (Compare both sources • Which provides greater historical insight into this enquiry, and why?)
Structure Strip: Para 1: Source A (Content + Provenance: King’s constitutional defiance) • Para 2: Source B (Visual Evidence + Context: military enforcement of regicide) • Verdict: Explain how the irreconcilable clash between divine monarchy and military sovereignty made regicide inevitable.
16/24 Charles I insisted no earthly court could try a king; three days later, Parliament had him beheaded outside Whitehall.

Stuart Source Workshop 4: The Bill of Rights & Sovereignty (1688–1689)

Question 3(a): How Useful [8 marks • 10–12 mins]
How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into how the Glorious Revolution (1688–1689) limited the powers of the English Monarchy?
SOURCE A: Parliamentary Statute • The Bill of Rights (December 1689) Contemporary Written Evidence
“That the pretended power of suspending of laws, or the execution of laws, by regal authority, without consent of Parliament, is illegal; That levying money for or to the use of the Crown by pretence of prerogative, without grant of Parliament, is illegal; That the raising or keeping a standing army within the kingdom in time of peace, unless it be with consent of Parliament, is against law; That election of members of Parliament ought to be free.”
Provenance Analysis:
• Nature: Landmark constitutional statute enacted by Parliament.
• Origin: Drafted by Convention Parliament and accepted by William & Mary.
• Purpose: Permanently abolish royal prerogative to suspend laws or tax without parliamentary consent.
1. Source A Evaluation • Content & Provenance: (What specific royal powers does Source A permanently take away from the English Crown?)
SOURCE B: Contemporary Painting • William III Landing at Brixham (5 November 1688) Contemporary Visual Evidence
Iconography & Visual Evidence:
• 1. Massive Dutch Fleet: 463 transport ships and 50 warships fill Torbay.
• 2. Armed Invasion: 15,000 Dutch soldiers and artillery disembarking.
• 3. Royal Standards: Flags display the arms of Orange and the motto ‘For Religion and Liberty’.
• 4. English Welcome: Local gentry and fishermen wading out to greet the Prince.
The Landing of Prince William of Orange at Brixham, Torbay (5 November 1688), leading a Dutch army to overthrow James II.
2. Source B Evaluation • Visual Evidence & Purpose: (How does Source B challenge the myth that the Glorious Revolution was merely a peaceful parliamentary discussion?)
3. Comparative Utility Verdict • Final Synthesis: (Compare both sources • Which provides greater historical insight into this enquiry, and why?)
Structure Strip: Para 1: Source A (Content + Provenance: statutory binding of royal prerogative) • Para 2: Source B (Visual Evidence + Context: armed invasion that forced royal collapse) • Verdict: Synthesise how military intervention produced the statutory constitutional monarchy.
In 1689, William III accepted the Bill of Rights to secure war taxes, permanently ending Stuart Divine Right. 17/24

“The execution of King Charles I in 1649 was the most decisive turning point in the struggle for power between Crown, Church, and Parliament in the period 1517–1689.” How far do you agree?

Complete Department Answer Bank • 24-Question Dual-Retrieval Key

Standardised Core Factual Knowledge & Causal Explanation Models (Enquiries 1–5 & Synoptic Turning Points)
Total Score: [        / 48 ]
Q1. Catherine of Aragon & Succession Crisis [2m]
• Fact: Catherine had no surviving male heir to secure the Tudor royal succession.
• Explanation: Henry feared a divine curse under Leviticus 20:21 and believed a male heir was vital to prevent civil war.
Q2. Pope Clement VII & Charles V [2m]
• Fact: Holy Roman Emperor Charles V sacked Rome in 1527 and held the Pope captive.
• Explanation: Charles was Catherine of Aragon’s nephew, so the Pope could not grant the divorce without enraging the Emperor.
Q3. Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533) [2m]
• Fact: It declared England an independent ‘Empire’ and banned legal appeals to the Pope.
• Explanation: This allowed Archbishop Thomas Cranmer to annul Henry’s marriage in England without Roman interference.
Q4. Act of Supremacy (1534) [2m]
• Fact: Declared Henry VIII ‘Supreme Head’ of the Church of England.
• Explanation: It permanently stripped the Pope of power in England, making denial of royal supremacy punishable by death.
Q5. The Title ‘Supreme Governor’ (1559) [2m]
• Fact: She adopted ‘Supreme Governor’ in the 1559 Act of Supremacy.
• Explanation: It defused Catholic objections that only Christ or the Pope could head the Church and placated Puritans.
Q6. 1559 Book of Common Prayer [2m]
• Fact: It combined Catholic (1549) and Protestant (1552) communion wording.
• Explanation: This ambiguity allowed moderate Catholics to imagine the Real Presence while Protestants saw a commemoration.
Q7. Papal Excommunication (1570) [2m]
• Fact: It excommunicated Elizabeth and released English Catholics from loyalty to her.
• Explanation: It transformed practicing English Catholics in the eyes of the Crown from religious dissenters into active traitors.
Q8. Babington Plot & Execution of Mary (1586–87) [2m]
• Fact: Intercepted coded letters proved Mary agreed to assassinate Elizabeth I.
• Explanation: Executing Mary in 1587 removed the rallying figurehead for Catholic plots and Spanish invasion schemes.
Q9. King Philip II’s Invasion Motives [2m]
• Fact: To restore Catholicism, avenge Mary Queen of Scots, and punish English privateers.
• Explanation: Philip viewed it as a holy crusade to depose Elizabeth and stop English military aid to Dutch Protestant rebels.
Q10. Drake’s Raid on Cadiz (1587) [2m]
• Fact: Drake burned over 30 warships and destroyed seasoned barrel stave supplies in Cadiz harbor.
• Explanation: This delayed the invasion by a full year and ruined Spanish food and fresh water storage at sea.
Q11. English Race-Built Galleons & Standoff Tactics [2m]
• Fact: English race-built galleons were faster, lower, and armed with long-range culverins.
• Explanation: English crews fired devastating broadsides from standoff range, preventing Spanish soldiers from boarding.
Q12. Calais Fireships & Battle of Gravelines [2m]
• Fact: Eight blazing fireships launched off Calais forced Spanish captains to cut anchor cables.
• Explanation: Scattered anchorless ships broke formation and were battered at Gravelines and wrecked by North Sea storms.
Q13. Divine Right & 11-Year Personal Rule [2m]
• Fact: Charles believed in the Divine Right of Kings and rejected parliamentary criticism.
• Explanation: Ruling alone allowed him to impose Arminian religion and unparliamentary taxes until the Scottish war bankrupt him.
Q14. Ship Money & John Hampden (1635–37) [2m]
• Fact: He levied an emergency coastal naval tax on inland counties during peacetime.
• Explanation: Landowners like John Hampden argued that taking property without parliamentary consent was illegal tyranny.
Q15. The New Model Army & Battle of Naseby (1645) [2m]
• Fact: It was England’s first national, professional army promoted on merit rather than birth.
• Explanation: Superior training, discipline, and Cromwell’s cavalry charges shattered the Royalist field army permanently.
Q16. Trial & Execution of Charles I (1649) [2m]
• Fact: Charles was tried as a ‘tyrant, traitor, and murderer’ and beheaded on 30 January 1649.
• Explanation: Having secretly conspired with the Scots in the Second Civil War, MPs concluded he could never be trusted.
Q17. The Restoration Settlement (1660) [2m]
• Fact: The military Protectorate collapsed into political chaos after Oliver Cromwell’s death.
• Explanation: The political nation restored the monarchy to recover social order, stability, and constitutional law.
Q18. James II & Dynastic Crisis (1688) [2m]
• Fact: The birth of a Catholic male heir threatened a permanent Catholic Stuart dynasty.
• Explanation: Protestant peers panicked that Protestant heirs Mary and Anne would be displaced by a Catholic succession.
Q19. William of Orange & Glorious Revolution (1688) [2m]
• Fact: Seven leading peers invited William of Orange; James II threw the Great Seal into the Thames and fled.
• Explanation: Parliament declared that by fleeing, James had abdicated, leaving the throne vacant for a constitutional contract.
Q20. The Bill of Rights (1689) [2m]
• Fact: It banned royal suspension of laws, unparliamentary taxes, and peacetime standing armies.
• Explanation: It permanently established parliamentary supremacy, transforming Britain into a constitutional monarchy.
Q21. Transformation of Crown vs Church (1517–1689) [2m]
• Fact: Religious power shifted from the Pope in Rome to Royal Supremacy, then statutory toleration under Parliament.
• Explanation: The Church was transformed from an autonomous Roman power into an institution regulated by English parliamentary law.
Q22. The Fundamental Struggle Over Taxation [2m]
• Fact: Monarchs claimed divine prerogative to levy taxes, while Parliament insisted only MPs could grant supply.
• Explanation: This dispute directly caused the Civil War and was resolved in 1689 by making unparliamentary taxation illegal.
Q23. 1649 Regicide vs 1689 Bill of Rights [2m]
• Fact: The 1649 Republic collapsed into military dictatorship and was overthrown in 1660.
• Explanation: The 1689 Bill of Rights established a stable statutory compromise that forms the basis of modern democracy.
Q24. Evolution of Parliament (1534–1689) [2m]
• Fact: Parliament evolved from a royal rubber-stamp under Henry VIII into the permanent supreme lawmaker.
• Explanation: Statutory guarantees of free elections, free debate, and taxation control permanently subordinated the Crown to the law.
⚠️ Common Examiner Traps & Key Historical Misconceptions GCSE GRADE 7–9 DISCIPLINARY PRECISION
1. Supreme Head vs Governor Henry VIII claimed absolute spiritual headship (1534); Elizabeth I deliberately chose ‘Governor’ (1559) to soothe Catholic conscience and avoid Puritan blasphemy claims while retaining legal governance.
2. 1642 Outbreak vs 1649 Regicide The Civil War was fought in 1642 to curb royal prerogative and enforce parliamentary consent, NOT to kill the King. Regicide in 1649 was a radical minority act after Charles secretly restarted war with Scotland.
3. 1688 Was an Invited Invasion 1688 was NOT a popular rebellion. Seven prominent English peers wrote a secret letter formally inviting Dutch Prince William with 15,000 troops; James II fled, allowing Parliament to claim abdication.
4. Cromwell: Protector, Not King Oliver Cromwell was offered the crown in the Humble Petition and Advice (1657) but refused it due to Puritan army pressure. He governed as Lord Protector, a military dictatorship, not an anointed monarch.
5. Ship Money Legal Nuance Ship Money was historically a lawful emergency tax on coastal towns during war. Charles I made it tyrannical by extending it permanently to inland counties in peacetime without parliamentary vote.
